Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.
papers.title: BabyTheorist: A Benchmark for Learning to Theorize the World from Observation Alone

papers.abstract: We propose a second-order, semi-implicit time-stepping scheme for the shallow-water equations on the sphere discretised with compatible finite elements. The scheme splits the advection operator from the wave operator, applying a DG-upwind SSPRK3 method to the advection part and an $H(\text{div})$-conforming implicit discretisation to the wave part, solved efficiently via hybridisation. The scheme follows a three-step symmetric splitting: an explicit half-step, a full advection step, and an implicit half-step that simultaneously projects the velocity back into the $H(\text{div})$ space. This symmetry guarantees global second-order accuracy and confines the stability restriction to the CFL condition of the advection step alone. The time-step can therefore be extended beyond this limit by subcycling the advection step without additional implicit solves. The method is implemented in Firedrake and validated against a standard suite of spherical shallow-water benchmarks, demonstrating stable results for Courant numbers up to 1 (with two advection subcycles) with second-order finite elements, second-order convergence, and good parallel scaling.
papers.title: A Second-Order Semi-Implicit Projection Time-Stepping Scheme for the Shallow-Water Equations on the Sphere Using Compatible Finite Elements

papers.abstract: LLM service selection requires performance evidence that reflects the demands of the current task. Aggregate scores obscure differences in capability and difficulty, while semantically related examples can involve different combinations of skills. We present RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure both the measurement of model performance and the selection of services. Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty, enabling alignment with corresponding model performance measurements. Historical requirements determine how outcomes contribute to global profiles and local capability estimates; incoming requirements determine how those measurements inform the current decision. A shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services. Evaluation across diverse tasks and heterogeneous LLM services shows that RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality. Comparisons with open Jev-style decision backends show consistent quality gains, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration. Ablations support the contribution of local performance evidence, while catalog-update experiments demonstrate effective reuse of the fitted scorer with refreshed model measurements.
papers.title: RouteAlign: Aligning Task Requirements with Model Profiles for LLM Service Selection

papers.abstract: Let $f:M^n\to\Sn^{n+q}(1)$ be a minimal immersion of a closed connected manifold with $n\ge3$ and $q\ge2$, and let $S$ be the squared length of its second fundamental form. We prove an integral inequality that gives $\max_M S\ge n$ if the immersion is not totally geodesic. If $n\ne4$ or $q=2$, equality $\max_M S=n$ holds if and only if the immersion is a Clifford minimal hypersurface; if $n=4$ and $q\ge3$, equality holds if and only if the immersion is a Clifford minimal hypersurface or the standard minimal embedding of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ in $\Sn^7(1)$. Both classifications are understood up to an ambient isometry, a totally geodesic inclusion, and a finite covering. We construct the integral inequalities using polynomial weights and divergence identities. The required algebraic estimates are proved by sums of squared tensor norms.
papers.title: The first gap for minimal submanifolds in spheres

papers.abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) is a long-established problem that aims to detect defects in industrial products during manufacturing for quality control. Most existing studies focus on static visual patterns as the basis for detection. However, in real manufacturing environments, many anomalies are dynamics-based, such as irregular movements that cannot be perceived from static cues alone. We observe that even recent Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based approaches fall short in identifying such dynamic anomalies due to limited temporal modeling capability. To address this, we introduce MUSTARD: MUltimodal SpatioTemporal Anomaly Reasoning and Detection, a framework that equips MLLMs with fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics awareness for detecting and reasoning about dynamics-based defects. MUSTARD introduces optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to capture critical motion irregularities through local motion patterns and global dynamic evolution. Its normal pattern-based reasoning pipeline requires only a few normal reference samples as the detection basis, avoiding any model updates. This enables efficient adaptation across various products and provides high decision interpretability. MUSTARD is the first MLLM-based framework for dynamics-based IAD. Experiments demonstrate its superior performance in detecting spatiotemporal anomalies and providing plausible explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/racercode/Mustard
papers.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics-Aware Industrial Anomaly Detection and Reasoning

papers.abstract: We find that MOF-5 supports both long-lived phonons and linker vibrations whose split spectra signal a breakdown of the phonon quasiparticle approximation. Combining mode-projected molecular dynamics spectra with spectral Wigner heat transport, we resolve two contrasting transport channels: low-frequency particle-like phonon propagation decreases strongly from 200 to 500 K, whereas wave-like phonon coherence remains nearly constant and supplies about half the intrinsic conductivity at 500 K. A phenomenological extrinsic scattering model provides a plausible explanation for the discrepancy between calculated and measured conductivities in terms of both its magnitude and temperature dependence. We also identify signatures of phonon quasiparticle breakdown in the linker vibrations of ZIF-8 and HKUST-1, indicating that this feature extends to other metal-organic frameworks.
papers.title: Heat Transport Mechanisms in MOF-5

papers.abstract: We record two observations concerning \cite{HLW24}. First, the proof of its Theorem~1 yields the population linearization (13)--(14) at \textit{any critical point} of the Fréchet function $F_μ$, under its remaining geometric and measure-theoretic assumptions; neither \textit{isolation} nor a \textit{nonsingular} Hessian of $F_μ$ is needed. Second, its Theorem~2 is given a shorter proof by applying the M-estimator theorem \cite[Theorem~5.23, pp.~53--54]{vdV98} to negative squared distance in normal coordinates, as opposed to the Donsker argument used there. We verify the pointwise differentiability, local square-integrable Lipschitz bound, second order expansion of population loss, consistency, and empirical maximization hypotheses. The resulting covariance retains the cut-locus correction. The same argument applies to a measurable selection of \textit{local} sample Fréchet minima when the population Hessian is positive definite.
papers.title: A Note on the Cut-Locus-Corrected Fréchet Mean Central Limit Theorem

papers.abstract: We study the asymptotic propagation speed of travelling wave solutions to the stochastic Fisher--KPP equation with multiplicative finite-activity pure jump Lévy noise, i.e.\ a compensated Poisson random measure of finite intensity, so that the solution evolves deterministically between successive jumps and jumps multiplicatively at the event times. Our main contribution is a stochastic Feynman--Kac representation for the solution, which expresses the random field as the product of the exponential martingale of the jump noise and an expectation over the paths of an independent Brownian motion. The representation converts the nonlinear stochastic partial differential equation into an expectation problem, allowing a direct analysis of the front position. Building on this representation, we derive sharp upper and lower bounds for the propagation of the front: for every speed $c>2\sqrt{1+a}$ the solution decays exponentially along the ray $x=ct$, while for every speed $c<2\sqrt{1+a}$ it does not. The two together identify the asymptotic speed in the critical-speed sense: the threshold between exponentially decaying and non-decaying fronts equals $2\sqrt{1+a}$ almost surely, an identity proved without any a priori existence of the limit $R_δ(t)/t$. The complementary bounds $2\sqrt{\underlineγ}\le c\le2\sqrt{\overlineγ}$ also hold, with $\overlineγ,\underlineγ$ explicit in $ε$ and $μ$. Under the finite-activity assumption, a stopping-time iteration yields pathwise $L^\infty$ bounds and finite-speed propagation of the level sets of the front, which underlie the existence of a travelling wave profile. The framework extends naturally to multi-species cooperative systems, and numerical simulations illustrate the informativeness of the speed bounds.
papers.title: Feynman-Kac Representation and the Asymptotic Speed of the Fisher-KPP Equation with Finite-Activity Jump Noise

papers.abstract: How often does an element of the geometric iterated Galois group of a Lattès map fix a vertex of the tree? Let A/K be an abelian variety over a separably closed field of characteristic 0, G <= Aut(A,0) finite, and alpha an isogeny of degree at least 2 normalising G. The Lattès map on X=A/G has a preimage tree governed by alpha-power torsion; we determine the fixed-point proportion in every dimension. For zeta in G the weight is the reciprocal of the number of fixed points of zeta in alpha-power torsion (zero if infinite); equivalently, it is a product of p-adic absolute values of determinants on the alpha-active subspaces; for scalar alpha=m the proportion is (1/|G|) times the sum over 1 != zeta in G of the product over p dividing m of the p-adic absolute value of det(1 - zeta | H_1(A,Z)). We deduce positivity and vanishing criteria, prove the groups G_infinity are martingale groups, determine the limit law, and reduce groups with translations to the fixed-origin case. In dimension one we determine ten values for scalar multipliers and nontrivial G <= Aut(E,0), and for the eight quadratic Lattès classes the proportions are 1/8, 1/4 and 5/16. Bridy-Jones-Kelsey-Lodge exclude the Lattès case from their main theorem; their Theorem 2.5 periodic-point bound is attained, via reductions modulo split primes p = 1 (mod 4), for the map (x^2+a)/(x^2-a), a^2 = -1, and we settle the exceptional case of the Fariña-Asategui-Radi conjecture.
papers.title: The fixed-point proportion of Lattès maps

papers.abstract: Post-training aims to enhance desired attributes in visual generative models while preserving their general generation capabilities. Reward-guided post-training faces two challenges: real training data may mismatch the generator's output distribution, and attribute supervision may be confounded by unrelated content. Unbounded reward maximization can also cause overoptimization and degrade generation quality. We propose a framework combining Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling (GARM) and Target-Aware Bounded Optimization (TABO). GARM mitigates distribution mismatch through generator-support matching and reduces content confounding using content-matched real contrasts, yielding generator-relevant, attribute-focused reward supervision. TABO maps the learned reward to a smooth, upper-bounded function calibrated from real target-positive examples. This transformation is independent of the optimization algorithm and supports both direct reward-gradient and policy-based optimization. We further introduce Target-Aware GRPO (TA-GRPO), an adaptation of Flow-GRPO that combines fixed stage-wise advantage scaling, a generator-to-target curriculum, and timestep-balanced credit assignment for flow-based video optimization. Experiments show that GARM improves target-attribute expression while maintaining competitive generation quality. TABO better balances attribute enhancement and visual quality than unconstrained reward maximization, while TA-GRPO improves target enhancement over vanilla Flow-GRPO and reduces unintended attribute leakage on neutral prompts. These results highlight the importance of generator-aligned reward supervision and controlled, data-calibrated optimization for targeted visual generation.
papers.title: Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling with Target-Aware Bounded Optimization for Visual Generation

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk and have made efficient video generation practical. However, further accelerating these models toward real-time generation remains challenging, as few-step distillation leaves little cross-step redundancy for existing training-free caching methods to exploit. We revisit this regime and identify two token-level redundancy patterns: cross-frame redundancy from static content shared across adjacent frames, and cross-step redundancy from tokens that converge early during denoising. Crucially, we find that early clean estimates along the model's own denoising trajectory provide an effective online signal for locating both patterns, requiring no retraining, auxiliary predictor, or reference video. Based on these findings, we propose PreSTP (Predictive Spatio-Temporal Token Pruning), a training-free framework that constructs a unified token-wise redundancy mask from cross-frame similarity and cross-step convergence. Tokens marked as redundant skip subsequent computation under a consistent last-computed-value restoration rule, and a content-adaptive mask reuse strategy further reduces dense probing cost. On 5-second generation, PreSTP achieves 1.52x-3.20x speedups and a better efficiency-fidelity trade-off than coarse-grained caching baselines such as TeaCache and FlowCache. On 30-second generation, it reaches up to 1.96x speedup while improving VBench-Long and suppressing long-horizon drift. Notably, it continues to reduce inference cost even in the extreme one-step regime, where cross-step redundancy vanishes entirely and coarse step-wise caching is no longer applicable.
papers.title: Training-Free Predictive Spatio-Temporal Token Pruning for Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion

papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal{L}$ generate a symmetric contraction semigroup. We prove a holomorphic Hörmander calculus on $L^p(X;\ell^q)$ at the optimal angle $\max\{\arcsin|1-2/p|,\arcsin|1-2/q|\}$, with boundary Sobolev order $s>3$.
papers.title: Holomorphic calculus on $L^p(\ell^q)$ with optimal angle

papers.abstract: Recent work in machine learning has demonstrated that transformer-based language model agents can communicate state not only through text, but also directly in latent space via key-value (KV) caches. In this paper, we argue that such cache-to-cache translation can provide utility beyond the original motivating application of real-time agent communication and can instead be utilized for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Building on the Cache-to-Cache (C2C) fusion framework, our proposed system CacheGraft encodes each corpus passage offline into a fused KV cache representation between a larger sharer model (4B parameters in our experiments) and a smaller receiver model (0.6B parameters) such that this cache can be injected into the receiver at query time with no need for the larger model. Across five QA benchmarks and two independent locally-run judges, CacheGraft improves answer quality over the text-only receiver baseline in 29 out of 30 comparisons, of which 17 of the 30 are statistically significant. Notably, these gains are zero-shot with respect to the fuser, which was never trained on retrieval data. These initial results suggest that latent-space document enrichment may be a promising avenue for enhancing the performance of RAG systems, particularly in compute-constrained settings where it is only feasible to deploy a small model at inference time.
papers.title: CacheGraft: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Latent-Space Document Enrichment

papers.abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.
papers.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?

papers.abstract: In this paper, we give diagrammatic descriptions of the quantum subgroups coming from conformal embeddings of the form $\mathcal{V}(\mathfrak{g}, \check{h}) \subset \mathcal{V}(\mathfrak{so}_{\dim \mathfrak{g}}, 1)$ for $\mathfrak{g}\in \left\{\mathfrak{so}_N, \mathfrak{sp}_{2N}\right\}$, as well as the conformal embeddings of the form $\mathcal{V}(\mathfrak{sp}_{2r + 2}, 2r) \subset \mathcal{V}(\mathfrak{so}_{\dim \mathfrak{sp}_{2r + 2}}, 1)$, extending the techniques of Edie-Michell and Snyder which applied to conformal embeddings of the form $\mathcal{V}(\mathfrak{sl}_r, r) \subset \mathcal{V}(\mathfrak{so}_{\dim \mathfrak{sl}_r}, 1)$. Our main conceptual innovation is the use of fermion condensation to construct a continuous family of planar superalgebras, which we call the Clifford BMW supercategories. The tower of endomorphism algebras, $CW_n(σ, ε)$ is a combination of Birman Wenzl Murakami algebras and Clifford algebras, much in the spirit of the Hecke Clifford algebras. This tower of algebras appears to be new, and already yields some exciting combinatorics.
papers.title: Clifford BMW Categories and Conformal Embeddings of Types B C and D

papers.abstract: Conditional independence testing is difficult when dependence is weak, localized, or expressed through distributional changes rather than a global mean shift. Existing tests usually return a scalar statistic or p-value, which can detect rejection but gives limited resolution about where the conditional law changes. We propose QRCIT, a quantile-resolution conditional independence test that compares P(X | Z) and P(X | Y, Z) through an amortized quantile deformation. A lightweight residual quantile-flow model first learns the baseline conditional quantile law and then learns the additional deformation induced by Y, yielding both a calibrated global test statistic and an inspectable deformation field over context and quantile level. We also introduce the Structural Dependency Benchmark (SDB), which evaluates real-world-inspired dependence structures, such as context-local, tail-only, sign-reversing, moving-ridge, and mean-neutral patterns. Across synthetic PNL and SDB benchmarks, QRCIT improves detection of structured alternatives while maintaining empirical Type-I control. Increasing quantile resolution consistently improves merged-SDB power, and the local-rescue strategy sharpens detection when dependence is concentrated in structural regions. On Sachs, METABRIC breast cancer, and CCLE/PLX4720, QRCIT provides competitive real-data performance and interpretable deformation patterns. These results support quantile-resolved conditional-law deformation as a practical framework for testing and diagnosing structured conditional dependence.
papers.title: Structural Conditional Independence Test via Neural Quantile Resolution

papers.abstract: Let $ C_ω$ be the cone generated by a proper $C^2$ domain $ω\subset\mathbb S^{N-1}$. We study positive homogeneous solutions of the fractional $p$-Laplace equation in $C_ω$ with zero exterior values. For $p\ne2$, the operator is nonlinear and not uniformly elliptic. For every $p>1$, we identify two extremal homogeneities $β^+>0>β^-$, prove that every fundamental solution, if one exists, has one of these exponents, and construct homogeneous eigenfunctions whose eigenvalues have signs determined by the position of the homogeneity relative to $β^\pm$. As an application, we obtain the Lane-Emden threshold $q^*=p-1+sp/β^+$ for every $p>1$: nontrivial nonnegative supersolutions of $(-Δ_p)^s u\ge u^q$ in $C_ω$ do not exist for $0<q<q^*$, whereas homogeneous supersolutions exist for $q>q^*$. We also establish Hopf-type lower bounds at conical boundary points with the optimal exponent. When $p-1>sp$ , we construct both fundamental solutions, one singular at the vertex and the other vanishing there. For $p=2$, these solutions are known; our method recovers them for every $s\in(0,1)$. The homogeneous eigenfunctions also serve as barriers, yielding boundary decay and global Hölder regularity for $(-Δ_p)^s u=f$ in bounded Lipschitz domains, with zero exterior values and $f$ continuous up to the boundary. The admissible Hölder exponents are determined by the exterior cones. All results hold for every $N\ge2$; in particular, $N>sp$ is not needed.
papers.title: Fundamental solutions of the fractional $p$-Laplacian in cone-like domains, with applications to Liouville-type theorems and global Hölder regularity

papers.abstract: Matrix optimizers such as Muon update whole weight matrices, which conflicts with the element- or row-wise sharding of data-parallel runtimes. Once parameters are sharded as well, matrix optimizers incur extra communication or repeated computation. We present DMuon, a matrix-granular optimizer runtime for PyTorch FSDP (ZeRO-2/3) and HSDP. DMuon assigns each matrix a unique owner, which performs the Newton--Schulz (NS) iteration and optimizer update on the full matrix, and balances the load across owners by computational cost. On HSDP, ownership is global across replicas, so the cluster keeps a single copy of gradients and optimizer state, and updated parameters are published across nodes as soon as they are ready, overlapping subsequent computation. This layout makes every collective sparse and variable in length, so DMuon schedules these collectives as their data becomes ready and routes them along the cluster's two-level network. On up to 256 H100 GPUs, across three dense LLMs and two VLA models, DMuon matches or exceeds the training throughput of PyTorch FSDP2 with AdamW, reaching 1.05$\times$ that of FSDP2 with AdamW at the median on 256 GPUs. The optimized parameter gathering and gradient reduction absorb the extra communication and computation a matrix optimizer requires. Against a gather-then-replicate Muon baseline, DMuon's throughput is 2.1 times as high at the median.
papers.title: DMuon-2: Scaling Matrix Optimizers in Data Parallelism with Topology-Aware Matrix Ownership and Communication

papers.abstract: Structural-response surrogates must capture moving resonances, phase changes, and unequal-amplitude transfer channels during optimization or health-state changes. Physics-embedded learning seeks FEA-level accuracy at lower cost by embedding physics in inputs, forward passes, losses, and backpropagation. We propose Modal Rational (MR), mapping structural features to modal quantities for analytical frequency-response reconstruction. The Physics-Guided Modal Operator Network (PGMON) adds bounded frequency, damping, and residual-flexibility corrections. Modal Operator with Structural GELU and Anchored-SIREN Correction (MOSAIC) denotes the bounded spectral-discrepancy framework used here; MOSAIC-MR and MOSAIC-PGMON add such discrepancies. They support finite-dimensional maps and physical decoders for future neural operators; evidence is fixed-topology, not a completed operator comparison. Two 20,000-design populations are studied: an 80 m steel truss tower with variable member areas and attached masses, and a tapered shell beam with ten variable station masses. Archived tests cover ten designs and seven acceleration histories per structure; they are benchmarks, not seismic-design assessments. With 5% reference modal damping, MR, PGMON, and MOSAIC give mean displacement-history errors of 0.73-0.76% for the tower and 0.029-0.116% for the beam, against declared band-limited modal references. Supplied modal frequencies are distinguished from design-only use; unequal parameter counts and training settings are explicit. Error analysis separates learned modal discrepancies, truncation, and excitation weighting, explaining acceleration and difficult-tower limits and risks of blind use. Results support physically structured prediction but limit claims about generalization, computational savings, and added corrections. Next is developing and validating neural operators around these architectures.
papers.title: A hierarchy of physics-embedded neural operators for structural dynamic surrogate modeling

papers.abstract: Video understanding models often rely on motion, yet their explanations can obscure which motion sources support a prediction. We identify motion-source under-specification as a limitation of existing video XAI: region-centric explanations can be source-ambiguous, while motion vocabularies restricted to single-person pose sequences are source-incomplete. We propose TraCE (Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding), a concept-based framework that discovers source-flexible motion concepts by clustering optical-flow trajectories from training videos. These concepts represent dynamic evidence from people, objects, and interactions, while object and scene concepts account for static context. The resulting typed trajectory/object/scene interface supports class prediction for action recognition and question-conditioned concept matching for video question answering (VQA). We evaluate TraCE across five random seeds on six benchmarks: NTU RGB+D Mutual, Chiral SSv2, UCF-101, KTH, TOMATO, and STAR. Relative to non-interpretable baselines, TraCE maintains competitive task performance, with an average accuracy drop of 1.0 points for action recognition and a nominal gain of 0.4 points for VQA. Motion perturbation and concept-removal tests provide complementary evidence of directional semantic alignment and decision faithfulness, while sample-level interventions illustrate targeted model debugging. Our project page is available at https://leewooil.github.io/TraCE_project_page/.
papers.title: TraCE: Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding

papers.abstract: Synchronous MoE reinforcement-learning post-training suffers from response-length imbalance. Existing methods reduce request tails, yet completed ranks remain bound to Expert Parallelism (EP) collectives and expert ownership. In a representative 16-accelerator Qwen3-30B-A3B rollout, this dummy run traps 32.83% of rank-time. AdaFloor converts this EP-coupled capacity into bounded leases for auxiliary work to improve system resource efficiency through rank-time reuse. Historical prompt-tail prediction and a calibrated guard construct the KV-safe layout. AdaFloor then selects the floor-specific safe quorum schedule with the largest predicted release area. Its runtime shrinks the EP group and leases detached ranks until full-world restoration. Across three updated-policy seeds on DeepScaleR mathematical reasoning rollouts, its capacity-oriented Natural floor2 configuration with TailGuard reduces Vanilla's 29393.9 rank-seconds of dummy run by 96.15%. Rollout shortening eliminates 18693.6 rank-seconds, while coordinated exits convert another 9568.6 rank-seconds into reusable capacity, leaving 1131.7 rank-seconds. For sidecar reuse, its Planned residency floor4 configuration without TailGuard serves 3134 Qwen3-8B GSM8K queries per epoch at 99.46% accuracy and incurs only a 2 to 3% primary throughput reduction against the same configuration with sidecar execution disabled. Its latency-oriented Planned residency floor4 configuration with TailGuard reduces rollout time by 24.09% relative to Vanilla and by 2.31% relative to LengthSort with TailGuard. On public Eurus-2-RL code rollouts with the same model and 16-rank topology, AdaFloor reduces rollout time by 20.56% and dummy run by 89.13% while generated work and mean reward remain stable.
papers.title: AdaFloor: Adaptive Floor Planning and Rank-Time Reuse for Long-Tail MoE RL Rollouts

papers.abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.
papers.title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory

papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for black-box mobile application testing, where the ultimate goal is the comprehensive coverage of the features users rely on. However, most existing studies focus on Activity Coverage, which measures the proportion of distinct application screens visited during a test session but does not directly measure whether agents actually test the features users care about. To address this, we focus on (1) how to automatically measure whether a testing framework covers the features users care about, and (2) how to design a framework that achieves more comprehensive feature coverage. To answer (1), we introduce the User-Centric Feature Coverage benchmark, which consists of two components: a manually crafted dataset of 3,012 user-centric target features based on real reviews and app descriptions, and an automated evaluation pipeline that translates agent-generated test cases and target features into a shared semantic space, then uses an LLM-as-a-judge to compute coverage. To answer (2), we introduce ECS (Exploration, Critical User Journeys, and Synthetic Reviews). ECS is a framework that explores the application, then uses an LLM to convert exploration traces into Critical User Journeys (CUJs) to bring the semantic meaning of the trace closer to a distinct feature. Each CUJ consists of an LLM-inferred user intent paired with reproducible test steps. ECS then aggregates multiple CUJs using persona-augmented synthetic reviews to capture more complex features, simulating real users who build knowledge of an application across multiple screens before writing a review. ECS achieves 64.1% feature coverage, a 23.8% gain over the state-of-the-art baseline, and covers 72.5% of features in app descriptions, capturing the most prominent features. Our failure analysis shows statelessness and exploration discoverability as main reasons of failures, providing future directions.
papers.title: Towards Comprehensive Mobile Application Testing for User-centric Feature Coverage via Simulating Real-World Users with Personas

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.
papers.title: From Pixels to Actions -- Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies

papers.abstract: Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2018) give $(1-1/e)$-competitive algorithms for matroid prophet-secretary and prophet-secretary with XOS valuation functions. In this work we show that these two guarantees have different limits. For every matroid, we give a randomized $(1-1/e+\varepsilon_0)$-competitive algorithm, where $\varepsilon_0=10^{-6}$. The guarantee holds for independent nonnegative values with finite expected optimum. For explicitly given finite distributions with rational values and probabilities, the algorithm has polynomial worst-case running time in the matroid independence-oracle model. The oracle tests whether a queried set is independent. The algorithm makes $O(N^4)$ such queries in expectation and $O(N^4\log(N+2))$ in the worst case, where $N$ is the number of elements. We further consider the i.i.d. version of this problem and provide a $0.6767$ competitive ratio for every matroid with i.i.d.\ nonnegative weights from a known distribution. This guarantee even holds in fixed arrival order (a.k.a. i.i.d. matriod prophet inequalities), even when the algorithm learns the order only as the elements arrive. For combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, however, we show that $1-1/e$ is the optimal competitive ratio. We give an explicit family of finite instances showing that no online algorithm can guarantee a larger competitive ratio than $1-1/e$, even when the buyers' valuations are i.i.d., every additive clause has coefficients in $\{0,1\}$, and computation is unrestricted. Thus the matroid improvement exploits structure absent from general allocation with XOS valuations.
papers.title: Prophet Secretary for Matroids and XOS Valuations: A Separation at 1-1/e and a 0.6767 Guarantee for I.I.D. Weights

papers.abstract: PageRank is widely used to quantify the importance of nodes in directed networks. In applications such as recommendation systems, it is increasingly important that the PageRank distribution provides a fair representation of node exposure. This motivates the problem of making minimal changes to a graph so that the PageRank values of a given set of target nodes $T$ match a desired vector $\boldsymbol{t}$. In this paper, we study this problem under an edge-addition budget $B$, where exactly $B$ edges may be added to the graph. We show that deciding whether a multiset of exactly $B$ added edges can make the target nodes attain their desired absolute PageRank scores is NP-complete. After this, we define the $\ell_1$ Target PageRank problem in which we seek to minimize the $\ell_1$ distance between the target vector and resultant vector. We show that this optimization problem admits no polynomial-time multiplicative constant-factor approximation unless $P=NP$. Motivated by these hardness results, we propose two greedy heuristics for approaching the target PageRank vector. We additionally propose a Random Walk Hungarian (RWH) heuristic that addresses the addition of edges between dissimilar nodes by incorporating a penalty for such edges. Finally, we evaluate the proposed heuristics on several real-world and synthetic datasets and compare their performance in terms of PageRank accuracy, computational efficiency, and the relevance of the added edges.
papers.title: Target PageRank: Matching Prescribed PageRank Scores via Budgeted Edge Additions

papers.abstract: Scientific image-analysis workflows require agents to select among diverse capabilities like description, detection, counting, and segmentation. Current multi-tool architectures conflate intent interpretation with visual execution, masking whether a failure arises from flawed reasoning (misrouting) or failed perception (invalid tool execution). This lack of auditability renders agents unreliable for high-stakes scientific automation. We introduce ZETA, an extensible architecture that operationalizes the decoupling of routing policy from action execution. ZETA resolves scientific intent before invoking specialized visual tools, treating measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry rather than generative output. This architecture exposes the "black box" of agent decision-making, allowing routing correctness and downstream execution to be evaluated as independent failure modes. To our knowledge, we provide the first controlled study in scientific vision-agent routing that isolates explicit routing-policy specification while holding the legal action interface fixed. Evaluation on a zero-shot benchmark of 51 scientific-intent queries shows that explicit routing semantics can substantially improve routing accuracy, particularly at semantically adjacent action boundaries, although improvements vary across models. For Qwen 3.8, explicit routing-policy specification improves segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%. ZETA's execution traces make routing decisions and downstream artifacts separately observable, providing a basis for distinguishing intent-selection errors from visual execution failures. ZETA establishes the necessary infrastructure to isolate execution errors from interpretive ones, a critical requirement for deploying reliable scientific vision agents.
papers.title: Route First, See Later: Enabling Vision Agents to Reason Scientifically by Separating Routing Policy from Action Spaces

papers.abstract: We examine how the geometry of rotating black holes in linear, shift-symmetric Einstein--scalar--Gauss--Bonnet (EsGB) gravity changes the limiting tidal equilibria of white dwarfs (WDs). The relativistic tidal field is obtained from numerical EsGB backgrounds in a parallel-transported frame and coupled to a compressible affine model. Comparisons with Kerr black holes matched in Arnowitt--Deser--Misner (ADM) mass and angular momentum show a positive shift in the orbital frequency at the tidal fold. At fixed spin the relative correction follows an approximately quadratic dependence on the EsGB coupling, consistent with the leading response of the metric to the scalar field. Over the sampled backgrounds, the relative correction reaches order $10^{-3}$. Black hole rotation also changes the relation between the tidal fold and the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO): the sampled prograde folds remain outside the ISCO, while retrograde folds move inside it at higher spins. Orbital orientation therefore controls whether tidal equilibrium is lost before the orbital stability limit is reached. For the stellar and black hole masses considered here, the characteristic gravitational wave (GW) frequencies fall in the millihertz band relevant to planned space based interferometers. Future GW observations capable of resolving deviations from Kerr predictions could constrain the EsGB coupling.
papers.title: Quasi-equilibrium tidal folds of white dwarfs around rotating black holes in shift-symmetric Einstein--scalar--Gauss--Bonnet gravity

papers.abstract: Finding high-performing formulations is difficult when few have been measured and experimental budgets are limited. We propose KolTa, an active learning framework that selects batches to discover the top 5% of formulations at a target temperature under a fixed query budget. KolTa combines a three-stage predictor of component contributions, role-conditioned interactions, and anchored temperature response with task-specific soft physics constraints. Its Physics-Residual-Calibrated Upper Confidence Bound (PRC-UCB) acquisition rule combines predicted utility, ensemble disagreement, and a target-temperature physics residual, with nonnegative exploration weights fitted to out-of-fold signed errors. We evaluate the framework on three measured tasks and one simulated task covering binary-mixture viscosity, drug solubility, ionic-liquid viscosity, and electrolyte conductivity. KolTa ranks first or second in mean area under the learning curve (AULC) on every task and outperforms seven of the eight comparator strategies in paired tests, winning 75 of 78 paired comparisons across tasks and seeds against those seven strategies. Across the three measured tasks, its largest gap to the best mean AULC is 0.032, compared with at least 0.056 for every comparator. On Drug, reaching 80% average recovery of the remaining targets across drugs requires an estimated median of 348 additional formulation queries, about 18% fewer than the fastest comparator. Researchers can adapt the framework to diverse formulation problems through component roles and physical constraints.
papers.title: KolTa: A Physics-Informed Active Learning Framework for Formulation Discovery with Limited Data

papers.abstract: At work, people develop skills through experience: novices acquire skills by completing tasks, while experts retain theirs through continued practice. AI assistance changes this process by offering workers a choice between solving tasks independently and accepting the AI's answers. While relying on AI saves immediate effort, it can also displace the practice needed to acquire and retain skills, including those required to oversee the AI. We extend an existing accept-or-solve model to a sequence of tasks in which workers' skills evolve through independent practice and reliance on AI. We compare myopic workers, who maximize immediate utility, with strategic workers, who also value their future skills. We show that novices can become trapped at low skill levels, while experts may lose skill, even as AI-assisted outcome accuracy remains high. Strategic workers, by contrast, may choose to solve independently even when AI is more accurate, recognizing the future value of acquiring and retaining their skills. We then study incentives that reward correct independent work and characterize the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention. We show that independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire sufficient skill, eliminating the need for continued incentives. Counterintuitively, supporting a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs, either by enabling self-sustaining independent work or by lowering the payments needed to maintain proficiency. Our findings thereby shift the focus from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations can sustain human expertise over time, and which skills are worth investing in.
papers.title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work

papers.abstract: A central challenge in AI is specifying objectives that align with human preferences. While existing theoretical results elucidate how misspecification impacts performance, they typically do not distinguish between merely suboptimal and catastrophic outcomes. To enable rigorous analysis of catastrophic risk from AI misalignment, we introduce a formal definition of catastrophic performance. Our definition is based on two reference values. The first, baseline value, captures the value attained if no agent is deployed. The second, orthogonal value, captures the value of a trajectory that is unrelated to human preferences, in a sense we describe. Orthogonal value is typically far worse than baseline value. We interpret these reference values through examples in which past human activity has altered the state of the environment to human benefit. Starting at the resulting state, an AI agent is deployed with the goal of accelerating further progress. Catastrophic performance represents this agent's undoing of benefits afforded by human activity.
papers.title: A Definition of Catastrophic Performance

papers.abstract: Multivariate probabilistic forecasting requires modeling cross-variable dependence alongside marginal uncertainty. The challenge is to learn this dependence while controlling marginal noise scales and avoiding dense covariance costs. We propose Factor-Correlated Diffusion (FaCoDiff), which couples a compact conditional statistical estimator with structured denoising. History-conditioned factor loadings use distinct coefficients for forecast-center correction, scale adjustment and noise dependence. Diagonal compensation preserves the estimated marginal noise variances, while low-rank operators enable residual Gaussian likelihood evaluation and noise transport without dense covariance storage or factorization. Factor-derived feature modulation explicitly conditions the denoiser, and a geometry-aware objective accounts for errors after noise transport. The same conditional geometry governs forward perturbations and reverse sampling. Across nine datasets, FaCoDiff achieves the lowest mean variogram score on eight datasets and ranks among the top two on 43 of 54 dataset-metric combinations in the reported comparisons. Matched ablations on Solar and Weather show that factor covariance improves mean Energy and Variogram scores under all four combinations of center and scale correction. Disrupting cross-variable sample pairings while preserving marginal trajectories worsens joint and aggregate scores on both datasets, demonstrating the predictive value of generated cross-variable dependence.
papers.title: FaCoDiff: Factor-Correlated Diffusion for Multivariate Probabilistic Forecasting

papers.abstract: RL for LLM reasoning often plateaus early as its policy sharpens. Policy entropy is studied as both a diagnostic and a control signal, but increasing it alone does not reliably change the eventual plateau in our experiments. We analyze RL's implicit target policy using a sharpness factor $κ$ and effective counterpart $κ_{\mathrm{eff}}$ that describe how reward or advantage gaps translate into probability-ratio gaps. We introduce reward budgeting, a plug-in advantage construction assigning a fixed total reward budget to each prompt. For binary rewards and independent on-policy rollouts, its expected unclipped score-function update is the exact gradient of a finite-$G$ concave objective with diminishing returns; its advantage gap decreases as more rollouts become correct. For general rewards, a shifted log-mean interpretation holds asymptotically under the stated regularity conditions. On Qwen3-8B and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, reward budgeting consistently improves RL baselines, with gains up to +12.50 on AMC23 and +10.00 on AIME24 and AIME25. These results support an update-dynamics view of premature convergence and substantial gains without explicitly preserving entropy. Code is available at https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/RewardBudget.
papers.title: Reward Budgeting Reduces Premature Convergence in Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning

papers.abstract: In present work, mass spectrum of the low-lying $cccq\bar{q}$ pentaquarks states with $q\bar{q}=u\bar{u}$, $d\bar{d}$ and $s\bar{s}$, are investigated employing a constituent quark model, within which the spin-dependent hyperfine interactions are taken to be the instanton-induced interaction and the one-gluon-exchange interaction, respectively. The model parameters are fixed by fitting the mass spectrum of the relative $q\bar{q}$ and $qqq$ traditional hadrons. The numerical results show that energies for all the obtained states in the two employed models are higher than corresponding meson-baryon channels, consequently, we roughly estimate strong decays of these states using a simple quark rearrangement model, the corresponding partial width ratios for different decay channels are presented.
papers.title: Investigations on the low-lying triply charmed pentaquark states in a constituent quark model

papers.abstract: Measurements of spin correlations and CP are an exciting and challenging part of the precision-LHC program. We first show how L-GATr-slim, as a Lorentz-equivariant transformer, significantly boosts the spin analyzing power for hadronic top quarks. We then show how adding a pseudoscalar channel to its architecture allows us to learn and interpret optimal observables and their CP properties. We demonstrate this for WBF-Higgs production at parton level and top pair production including detector effects.
papers.title: Top Spin and CP from Equivariant Transformers

papers.abstract: In this work, we employed the modified Godfrey--Isgur model to systematically investigate the mass spectra of several light, heavy-light, and heavy-heavy meson systems. In this model, a screened potential is employed to phenomenologically account for modifications to the long-range confining interaction associated with unquenched effects. We performed a global refit of the relevant model parameters to a combined set of 90 adopted meson masses spanning all three sectors, ensuring a consistent parameter determination across the different meson systems. Using the resulting parameter set, we calculated the low-lying and highly excited spectra and the corresponding mixed states in different meson families, and compared our results with existing experimental data and other theoretical results. The assignment of several newly observed structures (such as $B_c^*$ and $D_{s1}(2933)$) have also been discussed based on their predicted masses. Overall, the model describes several main spectroscopic features across different flavors and provides mass predictions for highly excited states that have not yet been experimentally established.
papers.title: Meson spectra in a screened relativized quark model

papers.abstract: We prove that every finite simple graph $G$ with maximum degree at least $750$ satisfies $χ(G)\le\max\{ω(G),Δ(G)-1\}$. The proof starts with a random partial colouring and completes it on large cliques using a list-colouring condition that remains valid as the rest of the graph is coloured. Disjoint stars provide the required colours. We estimate the number of stars that can be chosen after the clique colours have been exposed, while keeping their endpoint set fixed. A common exponential-moment argument reduces intervals of packing sizes to endpoint comparisons. More detailed neighbourhood estimates handle the remaining vertices. The final probability inequalities are verified by directed rational and interval arithmetic.
papers.title: The Borodin--Kostochka inequality from degree 750

papers.abstract: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy$\unicode{x2014}$answers that are correct and in the target language$\unicode{x2014}$slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.
papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation involves not only moving objects, but also arranging the hand around them to maintain useful contacts and enable subsequent actions. Yet many learning-based systems specify goals primarily through object poses or trajectories, leaving hand-object configurations to emerge implicitly. We introduce DexHOT, which formulates dexterous manipulation as hand-object configuration transfer: moving between feasible configurations that jointly specify hand articulation and object pose relative to the wrist. DexHOT learns a reusable relation-conditioned transfer primitive from synthetic feasible configuration pairs, without human reference motions, and composes long-horizon behaviors through closed-loop tracking of configuration subgoals. On DexHOTBench with 120 objects, a single policy achieves 80.5% transfer success on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen objects; on a real dexterous hand, it achieves 61.5% success over 200 real-robot transfers and 90% task success across six demonstration-guided tasks. These results show that explicit hand-object goals provide an expressive and composable interface for dexterous manipulation. More details and videos are available at https://dex-hot.github.io/.
papers.title: DexHOT: Learning Hand-Object Configuration Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation

papers.abstract: Despite decades of progress, image codecs remain difficult to adapt to diverse real-world compression scenarios for two main reasons. First, most image codecs are optimized for a specific objective and require substantial redevelopment when the compression goal changes. Second, they typically assume clean inputs, whereas sensor-captured images often contain degradations that alter rate-quality behavior. To address these challenges, we propose Practical Image Coding Agents (PICA), a multi-agent framework that adapts existing codecs to diverse user requirements and potentially degraded inputs. PICA consists of four collaborative agents: a Perception agent that interprets user intent and analyzes image content, an Improvement agent that jointly considers bitrate and reconstruction quality to guide pre-coding restoration, a Coding agent that refines quality-control settings from global to regional levels, and an After-coding improvement agent that addresses residual degradations and compression-induced artifacts through restoration guided solely by image quality. To enable codec-agnostic regional adaptation, we introduce Agentic ROI Coding (AROIC), which treats the codec as a black box and allows the agent to automatically schedule, execute, evaluate, and reflect ROI coding plans without architectural modifications or codec-specific retraining. We integrate these four agents with a Scenario-Guided Quality-Rate (SGQR) evaluation strategy to enable more effective scenario-adaptive compression across heterogeneous codecs. Comprehensive experiments on clean, noisy, and blurred images across standard, perceptual, and machine-vision compression scenarios demonstrate that PICA consistently enhances the compression performance of both the conventional H.266/VVC codec and the neural Cheng2020 codec, outperforming competing compression methods on the Kodak, CLIC2020, and HEVC datasets.
papers.title: An Agentic Framework for Quality-Aware and Scenario-Adaptive Image Compression

papers.abstract: Photonic pseudospins enable selective excitation and routing of light, but perturbations that mix opposite pseudospins can induce backscattering in helical edge channels. Here, we experimentally demonstrate pseudospin-locked chiral edge transport in gyromagnetic photonic crystals, combining pseudospin selectivity with nonreciprocal unidirectional propagation. By jointly engineering lattice deformation and magnetic bias, we control dipolar-quadrupolar band inversions and construct interfaces supporting pseudospin-selective chiral channels. Microwave near-field and transmission measurements reveal a single chiral edge branch that is selectively excited by only one source handedness and exhibits pronounced nonreciprocal transport. Extending this mechanism to multidomain structures, we combine two pseudospin channels into a common waveguide, separate them into distinct outputs, and route them through intersecting interfaces. These configurations realize a nonreciprocal photonic pseudospin multiplexer and demultiplexer, together with a waveguide crossing exhibiting average measured crosstalk of -14.1 and -15.8 dB for its two input channels. Our results present an experimental route to integrating pseudospin-selective channel control with chiral edge transport, providing a foundation for nonreciprocal photonic networks that use pseudospin to organize and route multiple wave channels.
papers.title: Observation of pseudospin-locked chiral edge transport in gyromagnetic photonic crystals

papers.abstract: We investigate the circuit complexity of primordial scalar and tensor perturbations in the luminal branch of Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet (EGB) inflation. We construct the Hamiltonians from the quadratic actions and derive the evolution equations for the squeezing parameters. Although the tensor propagation speed is fixed to unity, the Gauss-Bonnet (GB) coupling remains dynamical through the scalar and tensor pump fields. We then calculate the Nielsen circuit complexity of the corresponding two-mode squeezed states. The GB correction produces a clear separation between the squeezing amplitudes, while the squeezing angles remain nearly phase locked. Therefore, the circuit complexity is mainly controlled by the evolution of the squeezing amplitudes. For the benchmark parameters considered here, a positive coupling increases the preparation cost of the scalar Gaussian state but slightly decreases that of the tensor Gaussian state. The scalar sector is therefore more sensitive to the GB coupling, whereas the luminal tensor sector provides a cleaner probe of the pump-field mechanism. Their opposite responses provide a differential state-space diagnostic of the same EGB background.
papers.title: Circuit Complexity of Scalar and Tensor Perturbations in Luminal Einstein--Gauss--Bonnet Inflation

papers.abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.
papers.title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds

papers.abstract: JWST has revealed an unexpected abundance of z>10 galaxies and striking spectral diversity. Here, we model bursty star formation histories (SFHs) to explore how they shape this diversity and whether spectroscopy can discriminate between explanations for the UV luminosity function (UVLF) excess. We find strong burstiness ($σ_{UV}(M_h=10^{10}M_\odot)$~0.9 mag), increasing toward low halo masses, is required to reproduce the z~6 UVLF and observed fractions of galaxies in recent star formation upturns and downturns, traced by SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}$. This burstiness naturally reproduces UVLFs and SFR upturn and downturn fractions over z~6-11. With increasing redshift, we predict galaxies in recent upturns (SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}>5$) increasingly dominate the UVLF bright end, reflecting rising accretion rates and burstier low-mass halos. This results in higher median emission-line equivalent widths (EWs), bluer UV slopes and weaker Balmer breaks at fixed $M_{UV}$, while distributions of these properties broaden. We find the downturn fraction (SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}<0.2$) is particularly sensitive to stochasticity: increasing towards faint $M_{UV}$ if burstiness increases in lower mass halos, and evolving with redshift only if stochasticity does. However, the model underpredicts the z~14 UVLF, so we explore two models which match the UVLF: increased burstiness and increased star formation efficiency. From z=10 to 14, at fixed $M_{UV}$, increased burstiness predicts the downturn fraction increases by ~2x and the weak-emitter fraction (H$β$ EW<50Å) by ~1.5x. By contrast, the increased efficiency model predicts a constant downturn fraction and declining weak-emitter fraction. Overall, our results indicate burstiness is important for explaining spectral diversity and evolution at z~6-14, and that spectroscopic samples spanning a broad $M_{UV}$ range can establish its role in the z~14 UVLF excess.
papers.title: How bursty star formation shapes spectral diversity at high redshifts: breaking degeneracies in early galaxy formation

papers.abstract: We investigate connections between operator spectra, complex dynamics, and determinants for wreath product groups. For a nontrivial finite abelian group $G$, the natural action of $G\wr\mathbb Z$ on a rooted tree produces a family of operators with a recursive structure. Applying Schur complements to this family yields a rational map on complex projective space. We determine the projective spectrum--the parameter values for which the operator pencil fails to be invertible--as the union of the Julia set of this map and an explicitly described subset of its Fatou set. We also prove that the associated Koopman representation and the left regular representation are weakly equivalent and therefore give the same projective spectrum. We then compute Fuglede--Kadison determinants for a family of operators on more general wreath products. These formulas yield injective operators with zero determinant for wreath products $K\wr\mathbb Z$, where $K$ is a discrete group admitting a nontrivial projection $e\in\mathbb C[K]$. This answers negatively a question of Li and Thom about whether injectivity implies positive determinant for operators defined by matrices over complex group rings of amenable groups. For $G_{tf}\rtimes_σ\mathbb Z$, where $G_{tf}$ is any countable torsion-free abelian group and $σ\in\operatorname{Aut}(G_{tf})$, we prove that injectivity does imply positive determinant in every matrix size.
papers.title: Spectral Dynamics and Fuglede--Kadison Determinants for Wreath Products

papers.abstract: Understanding how neurons respond to visual stimulus is an important question in both deep learning and neuroscience. It has significant implications for enhancing the interpretability of black-box artificial neural networks and for understanding the visual representation in the human brain. We propose a structured visual representations landscape and design an activation-based prior that allows us to effectively regularize the landscape with activations from brain regions or neural network units. Our model Vis-Lens integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model into an image generation framework. It enables the generation of natural, realistic preferred images by directly modifying the activation-regularized latent codes without per-image iterative optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on both artificial neural networks and human visual cortex using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Our framework improves activation modulation and image realism compared with a recent state-of-the-art method for generating preferred visual representations of these neural targets. Code is available at https://github.com/NeuroAIHub/Vis-Lens.
papers.title: Structured Visual Landscape: Generating Preferred Representations in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks

papers.abstract: We investigate localization in a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattice with a real quasiperiodic onsite potential of strength $W$ and a staggered imaginary quasiperiodic modulation of strength $λ$. Using the inverse participation ratio (IPR), normalized participation ratio (NPR), fractal dimension $D_2$, transfer-matrix Lyapunov exponent, and wave-packet dynamics, we find a strongly non-monotonic and state-dependent response. At fixed $λ$, varying $W$ yields two distinct delocalization windows, whereas varying $λ$ at fixed $W$ produces a single re-entrant delocalization window. These regimes arise within selected eigenstate sectors, where localized states coexist with extended or critical states, leading to mobility-edge-like behavior. The corresponding suppression of the Lyapunov exponent and enhancement of the dynamical RMS spreading are consistent with the IPR, NPR, and $D_2$ results. Finite-size scaling confirms the persistence of the re-entrant features, while the complex-energy spectrum resolves their state-selective structure. The resulting phase boundaries delineate distinct localization regimes in the $(W,λ)$ plane. Our results show that the interplay between quasiperiodicity and a staggered non-Hermitian modulation sharing the same quasiperiodic spatial structure can generate re-entrant, state-dependent localization, with implications for localization and dynamics in non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattices.
papers.title: Multiple windows of eigenstate-selective delocalization in a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattice

papers.abstract: We study orthonormal Strichartz estimates at the critical coefficient exponent $q/2$ for fractional Schrödinger propagators. The proof for $d\geq3$ combines annular Schatten estimates with a frequency summation argument based on potential duality and Littlewood--Paley theory. In dimension two, a trace computation supplies the annular estimate needed for the global estimate. We also construct a counterexample to the global estimate with spatial $L^\infty$ and coefficients in $\ell^{q/2}$, even with a weak time norm.
papers.title: Critical orthonormal Strichartz estimates for Lebesgue spaces

papers.abstract: We investigate how far contemporary LLM-based agents can participate in multistep computational high-energy-physics research under reproducible human supervision. Using a previously published CEPC Bell-observable analysis in $e^+e^- \to ZH$, $Z \to q\bar q$, $H \to ZZ^* \to 4μ$ as a case study, we test two capabilities. First, the agent performs an instruction-constrained reproduction: it is explicitly instructed not to use the published numerical results as analysis targets, although no technical information-access barrier is imposed. The analysis definition is fixed before the formal comparison, and the resulting detector-level $I_3$ central values reproduce the four published benchmark points to within about 2% without retuning to those values. Second, the agent is used for an open-ended extension with no target answer supplied. Using 200,000 fast-simulated events, a stage-resolved audit identifies muon isolation as the largest single contribution to the hard-to-detector shift, and subsequent diagnostics connect the effect to angle-dependent isolation efficiency, proximity to the hard $Z \to q\bar q$ system, and mixed electromagnetic activity from muon final-state radiation and hadron decays. Throughout, the agent assists with workflow planning, code and configuration inspection, Monte Carlo production, anomaly diagnosis, control construction, statistical analysis, and result organization, while state-changing actions and final interpretation remain under human control. The study shows that the value of AI agents in HEP may lie not only in faster code generation, but in faster scientific iteration, and motivates systematic benchmarking across historical HEP analyses using correctness, human intervention, and researcher-time efficiency as explicit metrics.
papers.title: Towards AI-Agent-Accelerated Research in High-Energy Physics: A Case Study in Monte Carlo Analysis

papers.abstract: Parametric human body models such as the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) model provide compact representations of human shape and pose, but their reconstructions remain affected by both errors in estimated latent parameters and limitations in the decoder's expressive capacity. We propose a framework for refining these reconstructions by exploiting the geometric discrepancy between an initial decoded surface and a target mesh, without requiring vertex correspondences between them. The framework comprises three complementary approaches. Latent-VaRefine uses varifold distance gradients to correct the estimated latent code while preserving the original parametric representation. Vertex-VaRefine processes multiscale varifold-gradient features with a DiffusionNet backbone to predict vertex displacements in a canonical pose, yielding an approximately pose-equivariant refinement pipeline. ElaOpt directly optimizes surface deformations under elastic regularization and normal direction constraints. On AMASS, Vertex-VaRefine reduces the mean vertex-to-vertex error of OmniFit reconstructions from 1.181 to 0.342 cm, a 71.0 percent reduction, while combining Latent-VaRefine with ElaOpt reduces the asymmetric Chamfer distance of ArtEq reconstructions from 1.681 to 0.717 cm, a 57.3 percent reduction. Evaluations with SMPL-H and SMPL-X demonstrate the framework's adaptability to different body models, while additional experiments on remeshed targets and raw scans assess its robustness to changes in discretization and geometry beyond the parametric model. These results highlight the complementary strengths of latent space correction, learned vertex refinement, and elastic optimization, offering different trade-offs between preserving the model parameterization and improving geometric fidelity.
papers.title: Mesh-Agnostic Refinement Models for Latent Space Encoding of 3D Human Body Shapes

papers.abstract: People face the problem of classifying objects into categories while aggregating their opinions. We axiomatically study such a classification aggregation problem with multiple memberships, meaning that each individual assigns one category to every object, whereas the resulting classification may assign more than one category. Under the natural settings and axioms (i.e., Independence and Supportiveness), each of our new axioms -- Responsibility, Split Stability and Rejection Stability -- characterises what we call the junta rules. The rules assign a category to an object exactly when some member of a fixed coalition does so. The coalitions that can secure an assignment form a grill, a topological structure implied by an ultrafilter. Hence, the study parallels the literature on Arrow's theorem characterised by the decisive coalition structures. An infinite population setting is also investigated to clarify the differences among the axioms.
papers.title: Classification Aggregation with Multiple Memberships

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) serving places substantial demands on compute, memory capacity, and memory bandwidth. Economical accelerators can offer these resources at lower cost, but their limited per-device capacity requires pooling across devices, making communication overhead critical. We study cluster efficiency, measured in tokens per dollar and per joule, and show how low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnects enable economical accelerators to retain their cost advantage. Guided by a characterization of coding-agent workloads and accelerator scaling, we realize this design on the Tenstorrent Galaxy, a cluster of Blackhole chips. The serving stack combines integrated communication engines, pipelined ring transfers, communication-computation overlap, and device-side decode replay to reduce collective overhead. Across three dense models in BF16 and 8-bit configurations with 8K-256K-token contexts, the Galaxy achieves 1.07-2.24$\times$ the tokens per dollar of an eight-GPU RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell server under a three-year acquisition-and-electricity cost model. Emulating TCP-class communication on the same chips reduces throughput by 23.5-67.4% and eliminates the cost advantage in every evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate how fast interconnects translate the per-dollar resource advantages of economical accelerators into cost-efficient long-context LLM serving.
papers.title: Introducing Cluster Efficiency to LLM Serving: Pooling Economical Accelerators over Fast Interconnects

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models proposed in the literature outperform recurrent baselines, with the best-performing Transformer achieving BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, respectively, as well as ChrF = 18.09 and ROUGE-L = 10.51. These results indicate that the task remains promising and warrants further investigations.
papers.title: Maswao: An automatically collected, prepared, and benchmarked dataset for South African Sign Language

papers.abstract: The next generation of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys are designed to measure hundreds of millions of galaxy and quasar spectra, extending precision large-scale-structure cosmology to redshifts and volumes well beyond the reach of current Stage-IV facilities. Realising this potential requires revisiting the target selection strategies and designing them explicitly around the depth, multiplexing, and survey time of the new instruments, rather than a direct extrapolation of existing recipes. This work develops and characterises new strategies for the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), a proposed 12-metre, highly multiplexed facility expected to operate in the 2040s. Using deep multi-band photometry, including COSMOS-field data from CLAUDS and HSC, we revisit low-redshift $z \lesssim 1.6$ tracer selection of SDSS, BOSS/eBOSS, DESI and 4MOST-CRS -- Bright Galaxies, Luminous Red Galaxies, Emission Line Galaxies and quasars -- to photometric depth achievable in the WST era, and introduce a purely magnitude-limited sample (MagMax) exploiting three-dimensional color-color star-galaxy separation, and a set of Lyman-Break Galaxy dropout samples extending target selection to $z \gtrsim 2$. Using Fisher-matrix forecasts, we showcase the constraining power of a WST-like cosmological survey on BAO distance parameters $α_\parallel$ and $α_\perp$, the growth rate $f$, the evolving dark energy equation $w_0w_a$, the local-type primordial non-Gaussianity $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}$, and the sum of the neutrino mass $Σm_ν$. The main outcome of this work is an optimisation framework that directly links instrumental capabilities and observing time to cosmological constraining power, providing a science-driven template applicable to the design of future generations of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys.
papers.title: Targeting the future of spectroscopic galaxy surveys -- A cosmological study case with the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery from the literature requires assessing connections among findings obtained under different study conditions.
